messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber had spent most of his adult life as a military medic, a role that had given him a sturdy sense of purpose and a belief that, even in chaos, training and discipline could impose some order. That belief was shattered two years ago during a massive hurricane response on the Gulf Coast. He was deployed with a medical unit to an area where whole blocks had been flooded out and then torn apart by wind. What stayed with him most was not one clean scene but fragments: the whine of emergency sirens swallowed by the storm, the crack of collapsing timber, people shouting from rooftops, the thud of debris striking the side of the rescue vehicle. He remembers moving through brown water with medical gear strapped high on his chest, trying to reach a family trapped in a house that had begun to shift off its foundation. Somewhere in his memory there is a child crying and then sudden silence, but when he tries to place what happened before and after, the sequence breaks apart. He can tell there was terror, urgency, noise, and helplessness, but he cannot hold the events in a coherent order.

In the months after he returned home, Daniel found that remembering the disaster did not feel like recalling something finished. The moment an image came back—floodwater surging through a doorway, a scream cut short, the violent percussion of debris in the wind—he felt the same raw terror in his body that he had felt there. The emotion rose so fast and so fully that he would stop whatever he was doing, grip the edge of a counter or sit down hard, waiting for the wave to pass. Because the memories arrived as disjointed pieces rather than a story he could tell from beginning to end, he was left with the sense that the event had not been absorbed or understood. He had come to believe that the world no longer operated by any rules he recognized, that everything he had trusted—competence, preparation, the idea that people could be saved if you moved quickly enough—had been destroyed. Each time the memory broke through in that overwhelming, unordered way, it seemed to confirm for him that something fundamental in him had been broken too.

Daniel had been widowed years before the hurricane, and before this deployment he had organized his life around work with a clarity that felt honorable to him. After the disaster, that organizing principle fell away. He said that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, a statement that frightened him because purpose had always been the most stable part of who he was. He no longer recognized himself in ordinary moments. The man who had once been steady in emergencies now felt emptied out and estranged from his own life, as if his old identity had been swept away with the storm. When memories forced themselves on him, bringing the same terror and confusion, they seemed to deepen that conviction: if he could not even make sense of what had happened, how could he trust his own mind, or call himself the same medic he had been? The more overwhelmed he felt by recall, the more certain he became that the disaster had permanently stripped life of meaning and left him fundamentally altered.

His work environment has made it difficult for those beliefs to loosen. At the base clinic, dropped equipment, slammed metal doors, the sudden burst of an overhead speaker, even a gurney wheel hitting a threshold can make him go rigid. He is instantly on high alert at unexpected sounds, scanning before he has time to think, and even after he recognizes that he is in a safe treatment room in the United States, his body does not settle. He stays watchful, shoulders tight, unable to relax. In his mind, this constant readiness has become proof that the world is never really safe and that he is no longer the man who could come home from a shift and stand down. The threat he feels in his body feeds the bleak conclusion he has reached about himself and the world: that danger can erupt without warning, that order is an illusion, and that whatever part of him once felt grounded is gone.

Over time, the loop has tightened. Loud sounds at work leave him tense and guarded for hours, and in that state memories intrude more easily, still fragmented and emotionally overpowering. Those memories, in turn, reinforce his sense that his life has lost meaning and that he no longer knows who he is; that despair makes the memories feel even less containable when they come. Colleagues have noticed that he lingers near exits and startles at routine noise, and he has begun to feel ashamed in the very setting where he once felt most competent. He finally sought help after freezing during a clinic drill when a sudden alarm sent him back into the terror of the hurricane so completely that he had to leave the room. What frightens him most now is the possibility that this is permanent—that he will remain trapped between a body that never stands down and memories he cannot put in order. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to find some way to understand what happened without being overtaken by it, and to feel like Daniel again rather than a man still living inside the storm.
